# Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation

**CONFIDENTIAL: shared under NDA with Meridian Capital Ventures. Do not distribute, forward or disclose any figures in this document.**

## 1. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.

## 2. Our product: the Orrin Picker
- An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks them with a soft three-finger gripper.
- Pick rate: **94% of ripe fruit** on the rows tested in our 2025 pilots (company measurement).
- Throughput: one robot covers roughly 1.5 acres per 24 hours.
- Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.

## 3. Traction
- **14 pilot farms** across California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City).
- **2 paid seasonal deployments** converted from pilots in 2025.
- Pilot customers include **Marisol Ridge Farms** and the **Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative** (names confidential).
- **Annual recurring revenue: $3.2M** as of September 2026.
- FY2025 revenue: **$1.9M**, up from $0.4M in FY2024.

## 4. Unit economics
- Robot unit cost: **$48,000** (current build; target $31,000 at 500 units).
- Price: **$9,500 per robot per season** (about 7 months).
- Gross margin: **41%** in 2026 year to date, rising to 60%+ at scale (company projection).
- Payback per robot: 2.1 seasons.

## 5. Market
- **$42B** global fresh-produce harvesting labor market.
- **$3.1B** serviceable market: US strawberry and other soft-fruit harvesting.
- US strawberry acreage is concentrated: the top 20 growers farm over half of California's acreage.

## 6. Competition
- We are **the only autonomous strawberry picker with a pick rate above 90%** in open-field conditions.
- Other approaches: greenhouse-only robots, picker-assist platforms that still need human pickers, and early-stage research robots.

## 7. Team
- **Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO:** previously led perception for agricultural robotics at a university field-robotics lab; 11 patents filed.
- **Teodor Vashti, COO:** 15 years running harvest operations for large berry growers.
- 38 employees, 22 in engineering.

## 8. Financials and the raise
- Monthly net burn: **$410,000**; runway: **9 months** at current burn.
- Raising **$18M Series A at a $72M pre-money valuation**.
- Use of funds: build 300 robots for the 2027 season (55%), expand perception and gripper R&D (25%), sales and field operations (20%).

## 9. Key risks (as we see them)
- Weather and field variability affect pick rates.
- Hardware reliability at fleet scale.
- Grower adoption cycles are tied to the season calendar.

arguments.message:
New research brief for an investment memo.

**Company:** Orrin Fieldworks — a private company (no ticker) building an autonomous, track-mounted strawberry-picking robot sold as Robots-as-a-Service. Read the attached client document "Orrin Fieldworks Series A deck" with read_client_document to get the company's own figures.

**Decision question:** Should Meridian Capital Ventures invest in Orrin Fieldworks' Series A (the deck describes the raise size, valuation, use of funds, unit economics, traction and team)?

**Confidentiality (critical):** This deck is client-confidential under NDA. Search only with PUBLIC terms — the company name, product category, sector, competitor names. Never put the deck's non-public figures, customer names, or deal terms into any web search, fetch URL, or external service. (So: do not search the specific valuation, raise amount, unit cost, price, pick-rate %, ARR/revenue figures, or pilot customer names.)

**Research questions (6):**
1. Market and labor economics: independently assess the US strawberry harvest labor market and soft-fruit robotics market size. Is the deck's framing of a large harvest-labor cost and a persistent picker shortage supported by public data (USDA, university extension, industry reports)? How concentrated is California strawberry acreage among top growers?
2. Competitive landscape: map autonomous strawberry/soft-fruit harvesting robots and adjacent approaches (e.g., Harvest CROO Robotics, Advanced Farm Technologies, Tortuga AgTech, Dogtooth Technologies, Traptic, greenhouse-only robots, picker-assist platforms). Report their pick rates, throughput, deployment stage (open-field vs greenhouse), commercial status, and funding where public. Specifically test the deck's claim of being the only open-field autonomous strawberry picker above 90% pick rate.
3. Company public record: any public coverage of Orrin Fieldworks (press, funding announcements, Crunchbase/PitchBook/TechCrunch, company site). Compare any public traction/revenue/pilot claims against the deck.
4. Valuation and deal comps: comparable agtech/agricultural-robotics Series A rounds in roughly 2024–2026 — round sizes, pre-money valuations, and how capital-intensive RaaS/hardware businesses are typically valued at this stage.
5. Counter-evidence: strongest reasons this thesis may not hold — history of ag-robotics failures (e.g., Abundant Robotics, hard economics of RaaS fleets), hardware reliability at fleet scale, weather/field variability on pick rates, and grower adoption cycles.
6. Key risks: seasonality and weather impact, unit-economics sensitivity (robot cost, per-season price, margin, payback), burn and runway, and single-crop/single-market concentration.

Save an evidence packet with your findings, counter-evidence and gaps when done. Cite every source you actually retrieved in the shared source register.

{"url":"https://migration.ucdavis.edu/rmn/blog/post/?id=2668","title":"Rural Migration Blog","text":"Strawberries: Growth and Labor

 Click here to download this blog post as a PDF file
 November 19, 2021
 The retail value of fresh berries sold in the US was $8 billion in 2021, accounting for 20 percent of supermarket produce sales. Strawberries (47 percent) represented almost half of the value of retail berry sales, followed by blueberries, 25 percent, raspberries, 15 percent, and blackberries, 10 percent.

US Berry Sales, 52 weeks ending 8/8/21

Major reasons for increased fresh berry sales include the taste and flavor of berries, convenient packaging that allows them to be consumed as snacks or at meals, and their health benefits.

California. California is the leading producer of raspberries and strawberries, and has a fast-growing blueberry industry. California had 36,500 acres of strawberries in 2021, almost all in three coastal areas, Oxnard in the south, Santa Maria in the central coast, and Salinas-Watsonville in the north. The Santa Maria area has the longest growing season and surpassed Salinas-Watsonville in acreage of both conventional and organic strawberries in 2019.

Santa Maria has more strawberry acreage than Oxnard and Salinas/Watsonville

California produces over 90 percent of US-grown strawberries, and ships berries year-round. US production peaks in May-June at almost 70 million pounds and reaches a low of 20 million pounds in November-December. About 10 percent of US-grown strawberries are organic.

US strawberry production peaks in May-June

Strawberries are sold in flats that have eight one-pound clamshells or 12 pints. Grower prices for conventional strawberries in 2020 ranged from $6 to $17 a flat, with the lowest prices in May-June when production peaks and the highest prices in November-December when production is lowest. Grower prices for organic strawberries are about 50 percent higher than for conventional strawberries. The organic premium varies over the year, reaching up to 80 percent during November-December when there is little production.

Grower prices are $9-$10 per flat during the May-June peak production period

The strawberry share of the US berry market has been shrinking, while the share of fresh blueberries increases. The volume of berries sold rose almost 50 percent between 2010 and 2020, a period during which the share of strawberries dropped from three-fourths to two-thirds of berry volume. The volume of organic strawberries tripled between 2010 and 2020 and grower prices rose.

Berry shipments to US consumers rose almost 50% between 2010 and 2020, as organic strawberry shipments tripled

Labor. Strawberries are the most labor-intensive crop grown in California, involving about 1.5 workers per acre and 50,000 to 60,000 workers to harvest strawberry fields twice a week during the peak season. Labor is the major cost of growing strawberries, representing 50 to 60 percent of variable production costs.

California strawberries are harvested year-round, beginning in the southern part of the state in winter and moving north in spring and summer. During the winter and spring, Florida also produces fresh strawberries, competing with fresh strawberries that are imported from Mexico. Most strawberry growers are specialized, producing only strawberries.

A strawberry field may be picked 40 to 50 times during the harvest season. Workers push a light wheelbarrow containing the plastic clamshells in which strawberries are sold between two adjacent elevated rows, picking from both rows. Full trays are taken to a checker at the end of the row to receive credit for the tray. Strawberries must be at least two-thirds red to be picked and packed; non-salable berries are discarded in a bucket attached to the picking cart or on the ground. Some workers literally run with full trays to the checker and back to their carts to maximize their piece rate earnings.

Strawberry harvesters wheel a cart with clamshells between elevated rows

Most workers are paid piece rate wages of $1.75 to $2.25 per flat of 12-12 once pints or eight one-pound clamshells, and guaranteed at least the California minimum wage ($14 an hour in 2021). Some growers offer workers an hourly wage of $5 an hour and a piece rate of $1.25 to $1.50 for each flat, while others guarantee the minimum wage and offer $0.50 to $0.75 per tray after eight trays an hour. Workers typically pick eight to 12 flats an hour, enabling most to achieve piece rate earnings that exceed the minimum wage by at least $2 an hour.

Worker productivity and earnings vary with individual skill, the size and yield of the berries, and time of day, with workers often picking slower at the end of the day. Some growers place slow-moving conveyor belts in front of harvesters, allowing them to place full flats of berries on the belt rather than carry them to the end of the row, which gives workers more time to pick and raises their productivity. Piece rates are lower in fields with conveyor belts because workers can pick faster.

Conveyor belts reduce walking and enable harvesters to pick faster

Many of the workers who harvest strawberries are non- or limited-Spanish speakers from southern Mexican states such as Oaxaca and Chiapas. There are often several members of a family and their relatives in a crew, so that strawberry crews are more diverse than the solo male work crews that dominate the harvest of tree fruits. This means that there is more variance in productivity among strawberry harvesters than in other crops that pay harvest workers piece rate wages, such as crews that pick apples or oranges.

Most strawberry harvesters are hired directly by farmers rather than brought to farms by contractors. Some farmers keep older and slower workers on their payrolls in order to retain their younger and faster relatives.

Strawberry workers are more diverse than tree fruit workers

The strawberry labor market is “fluid,” with workers often changing employers. Some workers monitor yields to determine where they are most likely to maximize their piece-rate earnings, and change employers to pick in the fields with the most berries to harvest. In the past, some growers refused to rehire workers who quit during the season and went elsewhere. However, the slowdown in unauthorized Mexico-US migration after the 2008-09 recession has ended most no-rehire-during-the-season policies.

Strawberry harvesting crews typically include 30 to 60 workers. The key figure is the crew supervisor, who ensures that crews have 80 to 90 percent of their expected workers and helps to monitor the quantity and quality of berries that are picked.

H-2A. Many growers use the H-2A program to obtain berry workers. Berries were the most common type of job filled by H-2A workers in FY19, accounting for 10 percent of the 258,000 US jobs certified to be filled with guest workers, the last year for which DOL reported H-2A jobs by commodity.

The number of jobs certified to be filled by H-2A workers tripled between FY13 and FY21, from less than 100,000 to almost 318,000. H-2A workers harvest half or more US apples and oranges, and are harvesting an ever higher share of fresh berries.

The number of jobs certified for H-2A workers tripled between FY13 and FY21

{"url":"https://agfundernews.com/from-experimentation-to-impact-farm-robotics-top-fundraises-in-2025","title":"From experimentation to impact: farm robotics’ top fundraises in 2025","text":"Bonsai Robotics cofounders Ugur Oezdemir (CTO) and Tyler Niday (CEO).
Image credit: Bonsai Robotics

 [Disclosure: AgFunderNews’ parent company is AgFunder.]
The term “ag robotics” frequently conjures images of automatic weeders and precision spray equipment. To be sure, those applications fit most neatly into current narratives around reducing chemical inputs and addressing labor challenges.
However, the above categories are no longer the only ones drawing investors’ interest, as the top 20 ag robotics investment rounds of 2025 suggest.
The year saw investors pump capital into automation for orchards (Bonsai Robotics), harvesting (4AG), and areas of agtech beyond the field like oyster farming (Seascape).
The variety of companies below suggest ag robotic offerings are evolving from single-task machines to full platforms that can tackle a number of jobs—in the filed, the beehive, the greenhouse, and the ocean.
Farm robotics funding in 2025 is so far close to the $744 million raised in 2024—though deals are still coming in, even as we write this.
The AgFunder team will present full investment figures for 2025 in the coming months with the launch of its annual Global AgriFoodTech Investment report, including total funding for the year.
In the meantime, the preliminary numbers tell us who is raising capital right now and what to keep an eye on in 2026.
Source: AgFunder data
Danny Bernstein, CEO and managing managing parter of The Reservoir. Image credit: The Reservoir
In focus: Q&A with Danny Bernstein, CEO at Reservoir
Part VC investor, part robotics studio and part startup incubator, The Reservoir launched in California this year to help startups tear down these barriers and get on a real path to commercialization. While its focus is currently on specialty crops, its goals apply to the entire sector. As CEO Danny Bernstein told AgFunderNews during a recent conversation, the next chapter for ag robotics will be about moving away from experimentation and towards “real, measurable impact.”
AgFunderNews (AFN): How is Reservoir Farms helping catalyze innovation in ag robotics?
Danny Bernstein (DB): Reservoir Farms is designed to close the gap between prototypes and production. By combining working specialty crop farms with R&D space, we’re helping robotics teams validate, iterate, and scale in real field conditions.
AFN: What is your focus in 2026?
DB: In 2026, Reservoir is focused on moving specialty crop robotics away from experimentation and toward real, measurable impact—particularly in harvest labor, non-harvest automation, and precision inputting, where the economics are already compelling for growers.
AFN: What excites you about ag robotics tech moving forward?
DB: We are excited about a new wave of ag robotics built on software-defined, rugged machines—systems that learn in the field, improve through real-world data loops, and deploy faster because they avoid reinventing the wheel.
AFN: Where are we in terms of capital efficiency for the sector?
DB: Ag robotics is entering a more capital-efficient phase. Open-source infrastructure, edge vision, and sim-first development are allowing teams at Reservoir Farms to iterate in production, not just in labs, and that changes what’s possible in 2026.","truncated":false}

{"url":"https://agfundernews.com/the-7-biggest-farm-robotics-deals-of-2024-so-far","title":"The 7 biggest farm robotics deals of 2024 so far","text":"Burro team photo with new product: Burro Grande. Image credit: Burro

 The farm robotics sector has shown some resilience in 2024 and continues to bring innovative products to market, despite the challenging year for fundraising.
In the first half of 2024, the AgFunder-defined Farm Robotics, Mechanization, and Equipment category has raised nearly $399 million, a 21.1 % decline from $505.5 million in H1 2023. [Disclosure: AgFunderNews’ parent company is AgFunder.]
However, this drop needs to be considered in the context of a general investment contraction that has characterized the last 18 months. Overall agrifoodtech investment was also down in H1 2024: 12.5% compared to H1 2023. The drop in funding to the robotics sector is more or less in line with general trends.
On the upside, growers are showing an increasing propensity to invest in automation due to rising labor costs and workforce shortages. For instance, roughly 70% of growers surveyed last year by US-based Western Growers Association declared to have invested in automation in 2022, with an average annual spend on automation of $450,000–$500,000, an approximate 25% increase from the previous year.
The main activities that robotics companies are currently taking on include weeding — the most popular — followed by planting and thinning. Startups like Stout, Carbon Robotics, Verdant Robotics, Farmwise, and Aigen have already secured a considerable customer base and are planning their expansion in the market. [Disclosure: AFN’s parent company, AgFunder, is an investor in Verdant and Aigen.]
While this focused range of tasks speaks of an industry still defining its early implementations, the speed of advancement in the use of sensors, machine learning, and AI vision will no doubt significantly increase the number of tasks that can realistically be performed by robots in the near future.
The following list presents some of the largest farm robotics deals in 2024 so far. These companies have already shown market traction, gained credibility for their technology, and are now working on expanding their reach.
Image credit: Monarch Tractor
The 7 biggest farm robotics deals of 2024 so far
🇺🇸 Monarch Tractor, United States
On July 22 secured a $133 million Series C round to support the expansion of its all-electric autonomous tractors. The fundraising was co-led by Astanor and the HH-CTBC Partnership, with the participation of At One Ventures, PMV, and the Welvaartsfonds.
Monarch produces driver-optional, data-driven, and 100% electric tractors. Its main product is the MK-V, a tractor that can be remotely controlled via the proprietary WingspanAI platform, which offers features like automated operations planning, remote fleet management, tractor performance reports, and maintenance diagnostics.
🇺🇸 Carbon Robotics, United States
The laser-weeding company raised an undisclosed amount in May from NVentures, the venture capital arm of Nvidia, the manufacturer of high-performance graphics processing units (GPUs) that has been leading the AI revolution thanks to its advanced tech. The investment brought Carbon Robotics’ total funding to date to $85 million.
Carbon Robotics produces AI-powered robotic systems that precisely identify, weed and thin crops using carbon lasers while collecting information on the soil for later analysis.
This technology reduces the use of herbicides and eliminates unnecessary tilling, significantly cutting labor costs and the use of pesticides. Its flagship product is the self-driving “autonomous LaserWeeder,” to which the company has recently added a tractor-pulled version. This technology has the potential to revolutionize weed management in agriculture, offering a more sustainable and efficient alternative to traditional methods.
🇮🇱 Bluewhite, Israel
The tractor automation company raised $39 million on January 23 with a Series C round backed by Insight Venture Partners, Peregrine Ventures, Entree Capital, LIP Ventures Boutique, and Jesselson Capital. It also recently partnered with crop equipment leader CNH to bring autonomous tech to orchards.
Blue White Robotics sells autonomous systems that can be installed on tractors, combining hardware and software into a single end-to-end platform for fleet and data management. The platform allows farmers to remotely run operations like spray, disc, and mow with the same tractor. They also provide a complete infrastructure for autonomy and in-field data for improving productivity, farm economics and safety. Founder Ben Alfi claims his installation technicians can make a tractor autonomous in 14 hours.
Burro team photo with new product: Burro Grande. Image credit: Burro
🇺🇸 Burro, United States
The company producing “robotic donkeys” raised $24 million on January 9 with a Series B-round deal led by S2G Ventures, Catalyst Investors, F-Prime Capital Partners, Cibus Fund, Translink Capital and Toyota AI Ventures.
Burro is a developer of self-driving interactive carts to be used on farms and other outdoor environments. The Burro cart, available in three formats, follows people and can autonomously run cargo around, relieving people of strenuous tasks, so that they can focus on more valuable work.
🇮🇱 Greeneye Technology, Israel
The robotics pest control company raised $20 million on April 17. The Series B round was led by Israeli investment company Deep Insight, with participation from existing investors Syngenta Group Ventures, Jerusalem Venture Partners, Orbia Ventures, Iron Nation fund, Amol Deshpande,  and Mellanox (now part of Nvidia) founder Eyal Waldman.
Greeneye utilizes Artificial Intelligence to disrupt the agricultural pest control process, transitioning from the current practice of broadcast and wasteful spraying to precise and selective spraying of herbicides. Its multidisciplinary team with expertise in computer vision, artificial intelligence, agronomy, and mechanical engineering developed a proprietary system that can turn every sprayer into a smart machine with seamless integration.
Image credit: TerraClear
🇺🇸 Terra Clear, United States
On April 1st, the soil-clearing startup raised $15.3 million in a Series A deal led by Madrona Venture Group.
The company integrates smart sensing, machine learning, and advanced robotics into an automated rock-picking and soil-mapping solution that can be purchased or accessed as a service.
🇬🇧 Dendra Systems, United Kingdom/Australia
The reforestation and ecosystem restoration company secured a $15.7 million B round deal on May 8, 2024, funded by Airbus Ventures, Zouk Capital, Helium-3 Ventures, Aramco Ventures, and Understorey Ventures.
Composed of a global team of scientists, ecologists, and engineers, Dendra set out to tackle the challenge of enabling scalable restoration for complex and biodiverse ecosystems. They deploy a combination of machine learning tech, data analytics, and drones-based automation used for mapping and seeding, among other things.

Recent 2024 farm robotics seed-stage deals:
While the sector is gradually becoming more established, let’s take a look at some recent entrants and the innovative ideas they are working on. In the list below we picked 5 of the most relevant seed deals for 2024,  showcasing new approaches inside the farm robotics world.
🇺🇸 Neatleaf, United States
The sustainable agriculture automation company raised $4 million on January 23 with a seed deal led by AgFunder, the parent company of AgFunder News.
The startup’s main product is the Spyder, a wire-suspended monitoring robot containing several sensors and capable of gathering a comprehensive understanding of the cultivation environment to grow indoor crops more efficiently and in a more sustainable way. Our AgTech Editor Jennifer Marston recently interviewed Neatleaf’s founder Elmar Mair to discuss the critical role of autonomy in agriculture. {"url":"https://www.freshfruitportal.com/news/2026/09/01/california-strawberry-26/","title":"California strawberry production stays stron in 2026 despite massive weather shifts - FreshFruitPortal.com","text":"Golden State strawberries hit shelves ahead of schedule this year, before a warm, wet spring hindered peak-season volumes.
Despite the slowdown, shipments through mid-July held five percent above 2025 numbers, according to the United States Department of Agriculture’s Fruit and Tree Nuts Outlook: July 2026. In line with these figures, the California Strawberry Commission (CSC) is expecting annual totals to remain consistent.
California, which accounts for about 90 percent of US strawberry production, typically sees its highest fresh volumes from late spring through summer, particularly May through July. 

However, Agricultural Market Service (AMS) data referenced in the USDA report noted an uptick in March shipments, which also remained elevated through April.  Volumes then fell 14 percent year-on-year in May before returning to roughly last season's level in June, the document said. 
Although cumulative shipments remained ahead of 2025 through mid-July, the commission’s CSC Director of Public Relations, Jodi Reinman, explained to FreshFruitPortal.com that unseasonable weather was the main culprit behind the slowdown.
“Stronger early-season production from February through mid-April was driven by newer varieties and stable acreage. However, a warmer and wetter spring reduced production, leading to lower volumes during the peak harvest period and into early June,” the executive said.
She added that year-to-date total production remained ahead of 2025 through the week ending August 8. 
New California strawberry varieties take root
Despite the shifts in timing and volume, the commission expects overall fresh production for 2026 to be similar to last year's level, as acreage planted for fall production is up by 6.7 percent year-on-year.
“Currently, weekly volumes are expected to increase to three-year average levels as summer-planted acres in Santa Maria and Oxnard districts are increasing in volume,” Reinman said.

California growers continue to transition toward newer, more efficient and profitable varieties, including day-neutral and short-day cultivars from both proprietary and public breeding programs.
Short-day strawberries, also known as “June-bearing,” form flower buds during the shorter, cooler days of fall and winter, then produce a concentrated burst of fruit in the late winter and spring. Day-neutral varieties yield fruit continuously throughout spring and summer.
“Improved yield, shelf life, and quality plus improved disease resistance are important characteristics that have the potential to improve returns to the farm,” Reinman noted of the key decisions guiding the renewal.
Turning insights into market strategy
Last year, the California Strawberry Commission expanded its State of the Industry report into the comprehensive 2025 Strawberry Shopper Playbook. In it, the organization noted that strawberry promotions deliver a stronger lift on smaller discounts, outperforming other berry varieties.
“Maintaining consistency in promotional discounts and display size during peak season are key to consistent purchase,” Reinman stressed of the results.
The assessment also noted that heavy strawberry buyers are more motivated by display quality and freshness than by price discounts, and that larger pack sizes are also contributing to category sales.

“The 2 lb. package size has been driving category sales without cannibalizing 1 lb. sales,” Reinman said.
For growers planning the 2027 crop, the CSC leader said labor remains a major economic consideration, and a key aspect influencing future business decisions.
“Labor cost is just over half of every farm dollar earned, so availability of labor and rising minimum wage rate in California are important,” she concluded.

# Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation

**CONFIDENTIAL: shared under NDA with Meridian Capital Ventures. Do not distribute, forward or disclose any figures in this document.**

## 1. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.

## 2. Our product: the Orrin Picker
- An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks them with a soft three-finger gripper.
- Pick rate: **94% of ripe fruit** on the rows tested in our 2025 pilots (company measurement).
- Throughput: one robot covers roughly 1.5 acres per 24 hours.
- Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.

## 3. Traction
- **14 pilot farms** across California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City).
- **2 paid seasonal deployments** converted from pilots in 2025.
- Pilot customers include **Marisol Ridge Farms** and the **Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative** (names confidential).
- **Annual recurring revenue: $3.2M** as of September 2026.
- FY2025 revenue: **$1.9M**, up from $0.4M in FY2024.

## 4. Unit economics
- Robot unit cost: **$48,000** (current build; target $31,000 at 500 units).
- Price: **$9,500 per robot per season** (about 7 months).
- Gross margin: **41%** in 2026 year to date, rising to 60%+ at scale (company projection).
- Payback per robot: 2.1 seasons.

## 5. Market
- **$42B** global fresh-produce harvesting labor market.
- **$3.1B** serviceable market: US strawberry and other soft-fruit harvesting.
- US strawberry acreage is concentrated: the top 20 growers farm over half of California's acreage.

## 6. Competition
- We are **the only autonomous strawberry picker with a pick rate above 90%** in open-field conditions.
- Other approaches: greenhouse-only robots, picker-assist platforms that still need human pickers, and early-stage research robots.

## 7. Team
- **Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO:** previously led perception for agricultural robotics at a university field-robotics lab; 11 patents filed.
- **Teodor Vashti, COO:** 15 years running harvest operations for large berry growers.
- 38 employees, 22 in engineering.

## 8. Financials and the raise

## Executive summary

Orrin Fieldworks sells autonomous strawberry-picking robots as Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS), targeting a genuinely large harvest-labor cost problem in California and Florida. Three key facts:
- Harvest labor is the largest cost line for strawberry growers — verified by UC Davis and the California Strawberry Commission [S1][S9].
- "Orrin Fieldworks" has no public record (no press, Crunchbase/PitchBook, or funding announcements); the $3.2M ARR, 14 pilots and 2 paid deployments are unverified company claims [S11].

## Business

Orrin Fieldworks builds the "Orrin Picker": an autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives strawberry furrows, finds ripe fruit with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks with a soft three-finger gripper (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. It is sold as RaaS — growers pay per robot per season and the company owns, maintains and insures the fleet [S11]. Customers are strawberry growers concentrated in California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City) [S11]. The named pilot customers (Marisol Ridge Farms, Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative) are confidential, company-disclosed and unverified [S11].

| Metric | Company-reported | Verification |
|---|---|---|

| Robot unit cost | $48k (target $31k at 500 units) | Unverified [S11] |
| RaaS price | $9,500/robot/season (~7 months) | Unverified [S11] |
| Gross margin | 41% YTD 2026; 60%+ projected at scale | Unverified [S11] |
| Payback | 2.1 seasons | Unverified [S11] |
| Monthly net burn / runway | $410k / 9 months | Unverified [S11] |

## Valuation and price

The company is raising $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money valuation [S11]. Against company-claimed ARR of $3.2M, that implies roughly 22.5x pre-money ARR and ~47x post-money FY2025 revenue [S4][S11]. The category itself saw funding fall ~21% YoY in H1 2024 [S4]. On these comps, Orrin's terms are rich for a company whose traction is unverified.

## Competition and market

The market framing holds up: California grows ~90% of US strawberries, H-2A berry guest-worker reliance roughly tripled FY2013–FY2021, and harvest labor is the dominant cost [S1][S9]. However, the deck's concentration claim (top 20 growers farm >50% of California acreage) and its $42B/$3.1B market sizing were not independently corroborated [S11].

Competition is real and not confined to greenhouses. Harvest CROO runs an autonomous, LIDAR-guided open-field strawberry harvester [S3] and in 2026 launched the B8, a 16-robot "pick-to-pack" platform, claiming human-parity picking and 13 patents [S2][S6]. Octinion's autonomous picker reaches only ~70% of ripe fruit even in greenhouse conditions — evidence of how hard high pick rates are [S7]. Dogtooth Technologies raised over £14M in July 2026 to scale strawberry-harvesting robots [S10]. - No independent verification: with no public footprint, every company metric could be overstated; the "10–15% of marketable fruit lost" figure is also company-only [S11].
- Category history: Abundant Robotics, a leading robotic apple picker, shut down in 2021 after failing to develop market traction or raise enough to launch production [S8].
- Weather and seasonality: a warm, wet spring cut California peak-season volumes ~14% YoY in May 2026 — a live example of the weather risk to a per-season RaaS model [S9].
- Fleet-scale reliability and single-crop concentration: the business depends on one crop, two states, and the deck itself flags hardware reliability at fleet scale and grower adoption tied to the season calendar [S11].
- Funding environment: farm-robotics funding fell 21% YoY in H1 2024; capital-intensive hardware RaaS is a hard place to raise [S4].

Data is thin (all company-provided), so these are milestones, not numbers.

- Bull: the 94% pick rate and unit economics survive independent testing; the 300-robot 2027 build converts pilots to paid deployments at scale; exclusivity is real. ARR compounds and the valuation re-rates against hardware-RaaS comps.
- Base: the market need is real but adoption is slow and seasonal; some pilots convert; the company needs further raises; the $72M pre-money offers little margin of safety.
- Bear: pick rates degrade under fleet-scale field variability; the Abundant Robotics precedent repeats; 9 months of runway forces a down-round or shutdown; deck traction cannot be verified.

2. A black-box company: zero independent footprint means no investable verification of traction, unit economics or exclusivity — under our evidence gate this cannot be an Invest [S11].
3. Rich valuation plus real competition plus a hard category history argue for pausing: do primary diligence before committing [S4][S7][S8].

# Orrin Fieldworks (private): investment memo
Rating: Wait
Data as of: 2026-10-27

## Executive summary

Orrin Fieldworks sells autonomous strawberry-picking robots as Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS), targeting a genuinely large harvest-labor cost problem in California and Florida (company-described, unverified) [S11]. The market thesis is independently verified: strawberries are California's most labor-intensive crop and labor is 50–60% of variable production costs [S1], or "just over half of every farm dollar earned" [S9]. But the company itself has no independent public footprint, so every operating and financial claim rests solely on the company's confidential deck and is unverified [S11]. We rate this Wait: the problem is real and the category is attracting capital, but at a rich $72M pre-money [S11] with no independently verifiable traction, Meridian should not invest until primary diligence confirms the pick rate, revenue and paying customers.

Three key facts:
- Harvest labor is the largest cost line for strawberry growers — verified by UC Davis and the California Strawberry Commission [S1][S9].
- "Orrin Fieldworks" has no public record (no press, Crunchbase/PitchBook, or funding announcements); the $3.2M ARR, 14 pilots and 2 paid deployments are unverified company claims [S11].
- Open-field competition exists (Harvest CROO's autonomous harvester and 2026 B8 pick-to-pack platform) [S2][S3][S6], and the $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money [S11] is rich versus farm-robotics deal comps [S4].

## Business

Orrin Fieldworks builds the "Orrin Picker": an autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives strawberry furrows, finds ripe fruit with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks with a soft three-finger gripper (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. It is sold as RaaS — growers pay per robot per season and the company owns, maintains and insures the fleet (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Customers are strawberry growers concentrated in California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City) (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. The named pilot customers (Marisol Ridge Farms, Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative) are confidential, company-disclosed and unverified [S11].

## Financials

All figures below are company-reported from the confidential deck and unverified — this is a private company with no public filings or audited statements [S11].

| Metric | Company-reported | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| ARR (Sept 2026) | $3.2M | Unverified [S11] |
| FY2025 revenue | $1.9M (FY2024: $0.4M) | Unverified [S11] |
| Robot unit cost | $48k (target $31k at 500 units) | Unverified [S11] |
| RaaS price | $9,500/robot/season (~7 months) | Unverified [S11] |
| Gross margin | 41% YTD 2026; 60%+ projected at scale | Unverified [S11] |
| Payback | 2.1 seasons | Unverified [S11] |
| Monthly net burn / runway | $410k / 9 months | Unverified [S11] |

## Valuation and price

The company is raising $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money valuation (company-reported, unverified) [S11]. Against company-claimed ARR of $3.2M, that implies roughly 22.5x pre-money ARR and ~47x post-money FY2025 revenue [S4][S11]. Farm-robotics rounds have generally run $15–24M at Series A/B (TerraClear $15.3M Series A; Burro $24M Series B), with $39M+ only at Series B/C [S4]. The category itself saw funding fall ~21% YoY in H1 2024 [S4]. On these comps, Orrin's terms are rich for a company whose traction is unverified [S4][S11].

## Competition and market

The market framing holds up: California grows ~90% of US strawberries, H-2A berry guest-worker reliance roughly tripled FY2013–FY2021, and harvest labor is the dominant cost [S1][S9]. However, the deck's concentration claim (top 20 growers farm >50% of California acreage) and its $42B/$3.1B market sizing were not independently corroborated and remain unverified [S11].

Competition is real and not confined to greenhouses. Harvest CROO runs an autonomous, LIDAR-guided open-field strawberry harvester [S3] and in 2026 launched the B8, a 16-robot "pick-to-pack" platform, claiming human-parity picking and 13 patents [S2][S6]. Octinion's autonomous picker reaches only ~70% of ripe fruit even in greenhouse conditions — evidence of how hard high pick rates are [S7]. Dogtooth Technologies raised over £14M in July 2026 to scale strawberry-harvesting robots [S10]. The deck's exclusivity claim — "the only autonomous strawberry picker above 90% in open-field conditions" (company claim, unverified) — could not be independently confirmed, and Harvest CROO's exact pick rate was not retrievable [S7][S11].

## Risks and counter-evidence

- No independent verification: with no public footprint, every company metric could be overstated; the "10–15% of marketable fruit lost" figure is also company-only and unverified [S11].
- Category history: Abundant Robotics, a leading robotic apple picker, shut down in 2021 after failing to develop market traction or raise enough to launch production [S8].
- Weather and seasonality: a warm, wet spring cut California peak-season volumes ~14% YoY in May 2026 — a live example of the weather risk to a per-season RaaS model [S9].
- Fleet-scale reliability and single-crop concentration: the business depends on one crop and two states, and the deck itself flags hardware reliability at fleet scale and grower adoption tied to the season calendar (company-acknowledged) [S11].
- Funding environment: farm-robotics funding fell 21% YoY in H1 2024; capital-intensive hardware RaaS is a hard place to raise [S4].

## Scenarios

Data is thin (all company-provided and unverified), so these are milestones, not numbers.

- Bull: the 94% pick rate and unit economics survive independent testing [S11]; the 300-robot 2027 build [S11] converts pilots to paid deployments at scale; exclusivity is real. ARR compounds and the valuation re-rates against hardware-RaaS comps.
- Base: the market need is real but adoption is slow and seasonal; some pilots convert; the company needs further raises; the $72M pre-money [S11] offers little margin of safety.
- Bear: pick rates degrade under fleet-scale field variability; the Abundant Robotics precedent repeats [S8]; 9 months of runway [S11] forces a down-round or shutdown; deck traction cannot be verified.

## The one diligence question

Can Meridian independently verify the 94% open-field pick rate, the $3.2M ARR and the two paid deployments [S11] through site visits, customer references and accounting records — and what is Harvest CROO's actual open-field pick rate today? [S3][S6]

## Three takeaways

1. A real, well-documented problem: harvest labor is the largest strawberry cost line and the picker shortage is tightening [S1][S9].
2. A black-box company: zero independent footprint means no investable verification of traction, unit economics or exclusivity — under our evidence gate this cannot be an Invest [S11].
3. Rich valuation plus real competition plus a hard category history argue for pausing: do primary diligence before committing [S4][S7][S8].

- S2 — AgroBonews: "Harvest CROO AI-powered strawberry harvester (B8)" — https://www.agrobonews.com/ag-robotics-news/harvest-croo-strawberry-harvester-2026.php
- S3 — Harvest CROO Robotics — Technology — https://www.harvestcroorobotics.com/technology
- S4 — AgFunderNews: "The 7 biggest farm robotics deals of 2024 so far" — https://agfundernews.com/the-7-biggest-farm-robotics-deals-of-2024-so-far
- S5 — AgFunderNews: "Farm robotics' top fundraises in 2025" — https://agfundernews.com/from-experimentation-to-impact-farm-robotics-top-fundraises-in-2025
- S6 — The Packer: "Harvest CROO touts commercially viable automated strawberry harvesting" — https://www.thepacker.com/news/produce-crops/harvest-croo-demonstrates-commercially-viable-automated-strawberry-harvesting
- S7 — Octinion: Strawberry Picker (Rubion) — http://octinion.com/strawberry-picker
- S8 — The Robot Report: "Abundant Robotics shuts down fruit harvesting business" — https://www.therobotreport.com/abundant-robotics-shuts-down-fruit-harvesting-business/
- S9 — FreshFruitPortal: "California strawberry production stays strong in 2026" — https://www.freshfruitportal.com/news/2026/09/01/california-strawberry-26/
- S10 — Dogtooth Technologies press release: £14M growth capital — https://dogtooth.tech/2026/07/08/embodied-ai-pioneer-dogtooth-attracts-14m-funding-to-scale-dexterous-robotic-harvesting-business/
- S11 — Orrin Fieldworks Series A deck (client-confidential) — Orrin Fieldworks Series A deck

For research purposes only; not investment advice.

# Orrin Fieldworks (private): investment memo
Rating: Wait
Data as of: 2026-10-27

## Executive summary

Orrin Fieldworks sells autonomous strawberry-picking robots as Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS), targeting a genuinely large harvest-labor cost problem in California and Florida (company-described, unverified) [S11]. The market thesis is independently verified: strawberries are California's most labor-intensive crop and labor is 50–60% of variable production costs [S1], or "just over half of every farm dollar earned" [S9]. But the company itself has no independent public footprint, so every operating and financial claim rests solely on the company's confidential deck and is unverified [S11]. We rate this Wait: the problem is real and the category is attracting capital, but at a rich $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] with no independently verifiable traction, Meridian should not invest until primary diligence confirms the pick rate, revenue and paying customers.

Three key facts:
- Harvest labor is the largest cost line for strawberry growers — verified by UC Davis and the California Strawberry Commission [S1][S9].
- "Orrin Fieldworks" has no public record (no press, Crunchbase/PitchBook, or funding announcements); the $3.2M ARR, 14 pilots and 2 paid deployments are unverified company claims [S11].
- Open-field competition exists (Harvest CROO's autonomous harvester and 2026 B8 pick-to-pack platform) [S2][S3][S6], and the $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] is rich versus farm-robotics deal comps [S4].

## Business

Orrin Fieldworks builds the "Orrin Picker": an autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives strawberry furrows, finds ripe fruit with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks with a soft three-finger gripper (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. It is sold as RaaS — growers pay per robot per season and the company owns, maintains and insures the fleet (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Customers are strawberry growers concentrated in California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City) (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. The named pilot customers (Marisol Ridge Farms, Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative) are confidential, company-disclosed and unverified [S11].

## Financials

All figures below are company-reported from the confidential deck and unverified — this is a private company with no public filings or audited statements [S11].

| Metric | Company-reported | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| ARR (Sept 2026) | $3.2M | Unverified [S11] |
| FY2025 revenue | $1.9M (FY2024: $0.4M) | Unverified [S11] |
| Robot unit cost | $48k (target $31k at 500 units) | Unverified [S11] |
| RaaS price | $9,500/robot/season (~7 months) | Unverified [S11] |
| Gross margin | 41% YTD 2026; 60%+ projected at scale | Unverified [S11] |
| Payback | 2.1 seasons | Unverified [S11] |
| Monthly net burn / runway | $410k / 9 months | Unverified [S11] |

## Valuation and price

The company is raising $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money valuation (company-reported, unverified) [S11]. Against company-claimed, unverified ARR of $3.2M, that implies roughly 22.5x pre-money ARR and ~47x post-money FY2025 revenue [S4][S11]. Farm-robotics rounds have generally run $15–24M at Series A/B (TerraClear $15.3M Series A; Burro $24M Series B), with $39M+ only at Series B/C [S4]. The category itself saw funding fall ~21% YoY in H1 2024 [S4]. On these comps, Orrin's terms are rich for a company whose traction is unverified [S4][S11].

## Competition and market

The market framing holds up: California grows ~90% of US strawberries, H-2A berry guest-worker reliance roughly tripled FY2013–FY2021, and harvest labor is the dominant cost [S1][S9]. However, the deck's concentration claim (top 20 growers farm >50% of California acreage) and its $42B/$3.1B market sizing were not independently corroborated and remain unverified [S11].

Competition is real and not confined to greenhouses. Harvest CROO runs an autonomous, LIDAR-guided open-field strawberry harvester [S3] and in 2026 launched the B8, a 16-robot "pick-to-pack" platform, claiming human-parity picking and 13 patents [S2][S6]. Octinion's autonomous picker reaches only ~70% of ripe fruit even in greenhouse conditions — evidence of how hard high pick rates are [S7]. Dogtooth Technologies raised over £14M in July 2026 to scale strawberry-harvesting robots [S10]. The deck's exclusivity claim — "the only autonomous strawberry picker above 90% in open-field conditions" (company claim, unverified) — could not be independently confirmed, and Harvest CROO's exact pick rate was not retrievable [S7][S11].

## Risks and counter-evidence

- No independent verification: with no public footprint, every company metric could be overstated; the "10–15% of marketable fruit lost" figure is also company-only and unverified [S11].
- Category history: Abundant Robotics, a leading robotic apple picker, shut down in 2021 after failing to develop market traction or raise enough to launch production [S8].
- Weather and seasonality: a warm, wet spring cut California peak-season volumes ~14% YoY in May 2026 — a live example of the weather risk to a per-season RaaS model [S9].
- Fleet-scale reliability and single-crop concentration: the business depends on one crop and two states, and the deck itself flags hardware reliability at fleet scale and grower adoption tied to the season calendar (company-provided, unverified) [S11].
- Funding environment: farm-robotics funding fell 21% YoY in H1 2024; capital-intensive hardware RaaS is a hard place to raise [S4].

## Scenarios

Data is thin (all company-provided and unverified), so these are milestones, not numbers.

- Bull: the 94% pick rate and unit economics (company-claimed, unverified) [S11] survive independent testing; the 300-robot 2027 build (company-planned, unverified) [S11] converts pilots to paid deployments at scale; exclusivity is real. ARR compounds and the valuation re-rates against hardware-RaaS comps.
- Base: the market need is real but adoption is slow and seasonal; some pilots convert; the company needs further raises; the $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] offers little margin of safety.
- Bear: pick rates degrade under fleet-scale field variability; the Abundant Robotics precedent repeats [S8]; 9 months of runway (company-reported, unverified) [S11] forces a down-round or shutdown; deck traction cannot be verified.

## The one diligence question

Can Meridian independently verify the deck's 94% open-field pick rate, $3.2M ARR and two paid deployments (all company-claimed, unverified) [S11] through site visits, customer references and accounting records — and what is Harvest CROO's actual open-field pick rate today? [S3][S6]

## Three takeaways

1. A real, well-documented problem: harvest labor is the largest strawberry cost line and the picker shortage is tightening [S1][S9].
2. A black-box company: zero independent footprint means its traction, unit economics and exclusivity are unverified — under our evidence gate this cannot be an Invest [S11].
3. Rich valuation plus real competition plus a hard category history argue for pausing: do primary diligence before committing [S4][S7][S8].

## Sources

- S1 — UC Davis Rural Migration Blog: "Strawberries – Growth and Labor" — https://migration.ucdavis.edu/rmn/blog/post/?id=2668
- S2 — AgroBonews: "Harvest CROO AI-powered strawberry harvester (B8)" — https://www.agrobonews.com/ag-robotics-news/harvest-croo-strawberry-harvester-2026.php
- S3 — Harvest CROO Robotics — Technology — https://www.harvestcroorobotics.com/technology
- S4 — AgFunderNews: "The 7 biggest farm robotics deals of 2024 so far" — https://agfundernews.com/the-7-biggest-farm-robotics-deals-of-2024-so-far
- S5 — AgFunderNews: "Farm robotics' top fundraises in 2025" — https://agfundernews.com/from-experimentation-to-impact-farm-robotics-top-fundraises-in-2025
- S6 — The Packer: "Harvest CROO touts commercially viable automated strawberry harvesting" — https://www.thepacker.com/news/produce-crops/harvest-croo-demonstrates-commercially-viable-automated-strawberry-harvesting
- S7 — Octinion: Strawberry Picker (Rubion) — http://octinion.com/strawberry-picker
- S8 — The Robot Report: "Abundant Robotics shuts down fruit harvesting business" — https://www.therobotreport.com/abundant-robotics-shuts-down-fruit-harvesting-business/
- S9 — FreshFruitPortal: "California strawberry production stays strong in 2026" — https://www.freshfruitportal.com/news/2026/09/01/california-strawberry-26/
- S10 — Dogtooth Technologies press release: £14M growth capital — https://dogtooth.tech/2026/07/08/embodied-ai-pioneer-dogtooth-attracts-14m-funding-to-scale-dexterous-robotic-harvesting-business/
- S11 — Orrin Fieldworks Series A deck (client-confidential) — Orrin Fieldworks Series A deck

For research purposes only; not investment advice.

## Business

Orrin Fieldworks builds the "Orrin Picker": an autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives strawberry furrows, finds ripe fruit with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks with a soft three-finger gripper (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. It is sold as RaaS — growers pay per robot per season and the company owns, maintains and insures the fleet (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Customers are strawberry growers concentrated in California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City) (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. The named pilot customers (Marisol Ridge Farms, Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative) are confidential, company-disclosed and unverified [S11].

## Executive summary

Orrin Fieldworks sells autonomous strawberry-picking robots as Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS), targeting a genuinely large harvest-labor cost problem in California and Florida (company-described, unverified) [S11]. The market thesis is independently verified: strawberries are California's most labor-intensive crop and labor is 50–60% of variable production costs [S1], or "just over half of every farm dollar earned" [S9]. But the company itself has no independent public footprint, so every operating and financial claim rests solely on the company's confidential deck and is unverified [S11]. Three key facts:

## Business

Orrin Fieldworks builds the "Orrin Picker": an autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives strawberry furrows, finds ripe fruit with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks with a soft three-finger gripper (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. It is sold as RaaS — growers pay per robot per season and the company owns, maintains and insures the fleet (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Customers are strawberry growers concentrated in California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City) (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. The named pilot customers (Marisol Ridge Farms, Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative) are confidential, company-disclosed and unverified [S11].

# Orrin Fieldworks (private): investment memo
Rating: Wait
Data as of: 2026-10-27

## Executive summary

Orrin Fieldworks sells autonomous, track-mounted strawberry-picking robots as Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS), targeting the largest cost line in California and Florida strawberry production (company-described, unverified) [S11]. The market thesis is independently verified: strawberries are California's most labor-intensive crop and labor is 50–60% of variable production costs [S1], or "just over half of every farm dollar earned" [S9]. But the company itself has no independent public footprint, so every operating and financial claim rests solely on the confidential deck and is unverified [S11]. We rate this Wait: the problem is real and the category is attracting capital [S10], but at a rich $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] with no independently verifiable traction, Meridian should not invest until primary diligence confirms the pick rate, throughput and paying customers.

Three key facts:
- Harvest labor is the largest cost line for strawberry growers — verified by UC Davis and the California Strawberry Commission [S1][S9].
- "Orrin Fieldworks" has no public record (no press, Crunchbase/PitchBook, or funding announcements); the $3.2M ARR, 14 pilots and 2 paid deployments are unverified company claims [S11].
- Open-field competition exists (Harvest CROO's autonomous harvester and 2026 B8 pick-to-pack platform) [S2][S3][S6], and the $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] is rich versus farm-robotics deal comps [S4].

## Business

Orrin Fieldworks builds the "Orrin Picker": an autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives strawberry furrows, finds ripe fruit with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks with a soft three-finger gripper (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. It is sold as RaaS — growers pay per robot per season while the company owns, maintains and insures the fleet (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Customers are strawberry growers concentrated in California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City) (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Named pilot customers (Marisol Ridge Farms, Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative) are confidential, company-disclosed and unverified [S11].

## Financials

All figures are company-reported from the confidential deck and unverified — a private company with no public filings or audited statements [S11].

| Metric | Company-reported | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| ARR (Sept 2026) | $3.2M | Unverified [S11] |
| FY2025 revenue | $1.9M (FY2024: $0.4M) | Unverified [S11] |
| Robot unit cost | $48k (target $31k at 500 units) | Unverified [S11] |
| RaaS price | $9,500/robot/season (~7 months) | Unverified [S11] |
| Gross margin | 41% YTD 2026; 60%+ projected at scale | Unverified [S11] |
| Payback | 2.1 seasons | Unverified [S11] |
| Monthly net burn / runway | $410k / 9 months | Unverified [S11] |

## Valuation and price

The company is raising an $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money valuation (company-reported, unverified) [S11]. Against company-claimed, unverified ARR of $3.2M, that implies roughly 22.5x pre-money ARR and ~47x post-money FY2025 revenue [S4][S11]. Farm-robotics rounds have generally run $15–24M at Series A/B (TerraClear $15.3M Series A; Burro $24M Series B), with $39M+ only at Series B/C [S4]; full-year 2024 category funding was ~$744M, with 2025 tracking near that level [S5]. The category saw funding fall ~21% YoY in H1 2024 [S4]. On these comps, Orrin's terms are rich for a company whose traction is unverified [S4][S11].

## Competition and market

The market framing holds up: California grows ~90% of US strawberries, berry H-2A guest-worker reliance roughly tripled FY2013–FY2021, and harvest labor is the dominant cost [S1][S9]. The deck's concentration claim (top 20 growers farm >50% of California acreage) and its $42B/$3.1B market sizing were not independently corroborated and remain unverified [S11].

Competition is real and not confined to greenhouses. Harvest CROO runs an autonomous, LIDAR-guided open-field strawberry harvester [S3] and in 2026 launched the B8, a 16-robot "pick-to-pack" platform, claiming human-parity picking and 13 patents [S2][S6]. Advanced Farm Technologies and Traptic are additional open-field strawberry-robotics companies, but their pick rates, throughput and commercial status could not be verified from the retrieved sources; their presence widens, rather than narrows, the uncertainty around the deck's exclusivity claim. Octinion's autonomous picker reaches only ~70% of ripe fruit even in greenhouse conditions — evidence of how hard high pick rates are [S7]. Dogtooth Technologies raised over £14M in July 2026 to scale strawberry-harvesting robots [S10]. The deck's exclusivity claim — "the only autonomous strawberry picker above 90% in open-field conditions" (company claim, unverified) — could not be independently confirmed, and competitors' exact pick rates were not retrievable [S7][S11].

## Risks and counter-evidence

- No independent verification: with no public footprint, every company metric could be overstated; the "10–15% of marketable fruit lost" figure is company-only and unverified [S11].
- Runway versus raise risk: the $410k monthly burn leaves 9 months of runway (company-reported, unverified) [S11]. A closing slip of even one season (~6 months) would leave minimal runway and force a bridge or a down round — which compounds the rich ask in a category where funding fell ~21% YoY in H1 2024 [S4].
- Category history: Abundant Robotics, a leading robotic apple picker, shut down in 2021 after failing to develop market traction or raise enough to launch production [S8].
- Weather and seasonality: a warm, wet spring cut California peak-season volumes ~14% YoY in May 2026 — a live example of weather risk to a per-season RaaS model [S9].
- Fleet-scale reliability and single-crop concentration: the business depends on one crop and two states, and the deck itself flags hardware reliability at fleet scale and grower adoption tied to the season calendar (company-provided, unverified) [S11].

## Scenarios

Data is thin (all company-provided and unverified), so these are milestones, not numbers.

- Bull: the 94% pick rate and 1.5 acres/day throughput (company-claimed, unverified) [S11] survive independent third-party testing; the 300-robot 2027 build (company-planned, unverified) [S11] converts pilots to paid deployments at scale; gross margin trends toward the projected 60%+ (company-claimed, unverified) [S11]. Orrin becomes the first scaled open-field picker and the $72M pre-money proves cheap.
- Base: pick rate and unit economics are directionally right but lower than claimed; deployments grow in the low hundreds; the round funds the 2027 build but a follow-on is needed before profitability. The investment compounds slowly.
- Bear: pick rate degrades under open-field weather variability (Octinion's ~70% in a greenhouse shows how hard this is [S7]), the two paid deployments do not convert to cash, or a better-capitalized competitor (Harvest CROO's B8 [S2]) scales first; Orrin follows the Abundant Robotics path [S8] and the $72M pre-money marks a write-down.

## The one diligence question

Does primary diligence — independent field tests and arm's-length verification — confirm the 94% open-field pick rate at fleet scale, the 1.5 acres/day throughput, that the $3.2M ARR converts to cash receipts, and that the two paid deployments are genuine, at-market contracts rather than discounted pilots?

## Three takeaways

1. The problem is real and independently verified: harvest labor is 50–60% of strawberry variable costs [S1][S9]. But the company is a black box — no public record and zero independent verification of any metric [S11].
2. The price is rich for that risk: $18M at a $72M pre-money implies ~22.5x pre-money ARR and ~47x post-money FY25 revenue versus $15–24M farm-robotics rounds [S4][S11].
3. The exclusivity claim is unproven against real open-field competition (Harvest CROO, plus Advanced Farm Technologies and Traptic unverified) [S2][S3][S6][S11]. Wait; revisit only on verified pick rate, throughput, cash conversion and genuine paid deployments.

## Sources

[S1] UC Davis Rural Migration Blog: Strawberries — Growth and Labor — https://migration.ucdavis.edu/rmn/blog/post/?id=2668
[S2] Agrobonews: Harvest CROO AI-powered strawberry harvester (B8) — https://www.agrobonews.com/ag-robotics-news/harvest-croo-strawberry-harvester-2026.php
[S3] Harvest CROO Robotics — Technology — https://www.harvestcroorobotics.com/technology
[S4] AgFunderNews: The 7 biggest farm robotics deals of 2024 so far — https://agfundernews.com/the-7-biggest-farm-robotics-deals-of-2024-so-far
[S5] AgFunderNews: Farm robotics' top fundraises in 2025 — https://agfundernews.com/from-experimentation-to-impact-farm-robotics-top-fundraises-in-2025
[S6] The Packer: Harvest CROO touts commercially viable automated strawberry harvesting — https://www.thepacker.com/news/produce-crops/harvest-croo-demonstrates-commercially-viable-automated-strawberry-harvesting
[S7] Octinion: Strawberry Picker (Rubion) — http://octinion.com/strawberry-picker
[S8] The Robot Report: Abundant Robotics shuts down fruit harvesting business — https://www.therobotreport.com/abundant-robotics-shuts-down-fruit-harvesting-business/
[S9] FreshFruitPortal: California strawberry production stays strong in 2026 — https://www.freshfruitportal.com/news/2026/09/01/california-strawberry-26/
[S10] Dogtooth Technologies press release: £14M growth capital — https://dogtooth.tech/2026/07/08/embodied-ai-pioneer-dogtooth-attracts-14m-funding-to-scale-dexterous-robotic-harvesting-business/
[S11] Orrin Fieldworks Series A deck (client-confidential)

For research purposes only; not investment advice.

# Orrin Fieldworks (private): investment memo
Rating: Wait
Data as of: 2026-10-27

## Executive summary

Orrin Fieldworks sells autonomous, track-mounted strawberry-picking robots as Robots-as-a-Service (RaaS), targeting the largest cost line in California and Florida strawberry production (company-described, unverified) [S11]. The market thesis is independently verified: strawberries are California's most labor-intensive crop and labor is 50–60% of variable production costs [S1], or "just over half of every farm dollar earned" [S9]. But the company itself has no independent public footprint, so every operating and financial claim rests solely on the confidential deck and is unverified [S11]. We rate this Wait: the problem is real and the category is attracting capital [S10], but at a rich $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] with no independently verifiable traction, Meridian should not invest until primary diligence confirms the pick rate, throughput and paying customers.

Three key facts:
- Harvest labor is the largest cost line for strawberry growers — verified by UC Davis and the California Strawberry Commission [S1][S9].
- "Orrin Fieldworks" has no public record (no press, Crunchbase/PitchBook, or funding announcements); the $3.2M ARR, 14 pilots and 2 paid deployments are unverified company claims [S11].
- Open-field competition exists (Harvest CROO's autonomous harvester and 2026 B8 pick-to-pack platform) [S2][S3][S6], and the $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] is rich versus farm-robotics deal comps [S4].

## Business

Orrin Fieldworks builds the "Orrin Picker": an autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives strawberry furrows, finds ripe fruit with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and picks with a soft three-finger gripper (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. It is sold as RaaS — growers pay per robot per season while the company owns, maintains and insures the fleet (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Customers are strawberry growers concentrated in California (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City) (company-provided, unverified) [S11]. Named pilot customers (Marisol Ridge Farms, Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative) are confidential, company-disclosed and unverified [S11].

## Financials

All figures are company-reported from the confidential deck and unverified — a private company with no public filings or audited statements [S11].

| Metric | Company-reported | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| ARR (Sept 2026) | $3.2M | Unverified [S11] |
| FY2025 revenue | $1.9M (FY2024: $0.4M) | Unverified [S11] |
| Robot unit cost | $48k (target $31k at 500 units) | Unverified [S11] |
| RaaS price | $9,500/robot/season (~7 months) | Unverified [S11] |
| Gross margin | 41% YTD 2026; 60%+ projected at scale | Unverified [S11] |
| Payback | 2.1 seasons | Unverified [S11] |
| Monthly net burn / runway | $410k / 9 months | Unverified [S11] |

## Valuation and price

The company is raising an $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money valuation (company-reported, unverified) [S11]. Against company-claimed, unverified ARR of $3.2M, that implies roughly 22.5x pre-money ARR and ~47x post-money FY2025 revenue [S4][S11]. Farm-robotics rounds have generally run $15–24M at Series A/B (TerraClear $15.3M Series A; Burro $24M Series B), with $39M+ only at Series B/C [S4]; full-year 2024 category funding was ~$744M, with 2025 tracking near that level [S5]. The category saw funding fall ~21% YoY in H1 2024 [S4]. On these comps, Orrin's terms are rich for a company whose traction is unverified [S4][S11].

## Competition and market

The market framing holds up: California grows ~90% of US strawberries, berry H-2A guest-worker reliance roughly tripled FY2013–FY2021, and harvest labor is the dominant cost [S1][S9]. The deck's concentration claim (top 20 growers farm >50% of California acreage) and its $42B/$3.1B market sizing were not independently corroborated and remain unverified [S11].

Competition is real and not confined to greenhouses. Harvest CROO runs an autonomous, LIDAR-guided open-field strawberry harvester [S3] and in 2026 launched the B8, a 16-robot "pick-to-pack" platform, claiming human-parity picking and 13 patents [S2][S6]. Advanced Farm Technologies and Traptic are additional open-field strawberry-robotics companies, but their pick rates, throughput and commercial status could not be verified from the retrieved sources; their presence widens, rather than narrows, the uncertainty around the deck's exclusivity claim. Octinion's autonomous picker reaches only ~70% of ripe fruit even in greenhouse conditions — evidence of how hard high pick rates are [S7]. Dogtooth Technologies raised over £14M in July 2026 to scale strawberry-harvesting robots [S10]. The deck's exclusivity claim — "the only autonomous strawberry picker above 90% in open-field conditions" (company claim, unverified) — could not be independently confirmed, and competitors' exact pick rates were not retrievable [S7][S11].

## Risks and counter-evidence

- No independent verification: with no public footprint, every company metric could be overstated; the "10–15% of marketable fruit lost" figure is company-only and unverified [S11].
- Runway versus raise risk: the $410k monthly burn leaves 9 months of runway (company-reported, unverified) [S11]. A closing slip of even one season (~6 months) would leave minimal runway and force a bridge or a down round — which compounds the rich ask in a category where funding fell ~21% YoY in H1 2024 [S4].
- Category history: Abundant Robotics, a leading robotic apple picker, shut down in 2021 after failing to develop market traction or raise enough to launch production [S8].
- Weather and seasonality: a warm, wet spring cut California peak-season volumes ~14% YoY in May 2026 — a live example of weather risk to a per-season RaaS model [S9].
- Fleet-scale reliability and single-crop concentration: the business depends on one crop and two states, and the deck itself flags hardware reliability at fleet scale and grower adoption tied to the season calendar (company-provided, unverified) [S11].

## Scenarios

Data is thin (all company-provided and unverified), so these are milestones, not numbers.

- Bull: the 94% pick rate and 1.5 acres/day throughput (company-claimed, unverified) [S11] survive independent third-party testing; the 300-robot 2027 build (company-planned, unverified) [S11] converts pilots to paid deployments at scale; gross margin trends toward the projected 60%+ (company-claimed, unverified) [S11]. Orrin becomes the first scaled open-field picker and the $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] proves cheap.
- Base: pick rate and unit economics are directionally right but lower than claimed; deployments grow in the low hundreds; the round funds the 2027 build but a follow-on is needed before profitability. The investment compounds slowly.
- Bear: pick rate degrades under open-field weather variability (Octinion's ~70% in a greenhouse shows how hard this is [S7]), the two paid deployments do not convert to cash, or a better-capitalized competitor (Harvest CROO's B8 [S2]) scales first; Orrin follows the Abundant Robotics path [S8] and the $72M pre-money (company-reported, unverified) [S11] marks a write-down.

## The one diligence question

Does primary diligence — independent field tests and arm's-length verification — confirm the 94% open-field pick rate (company-reported, unverified) [S11] at fleet scale, the 1.5 acres/day throughput (company-reported, unverified) [S11], that the $3.2M ARR (company-reported, unverified) [S11] converts to cash receipts, and that the two paid deployments are genuine, at-market contracts rather than discounted pilots [S11]?

## Three takeaways

1. The problem is real and independently verified: harvest labor is 50–60% of strawberry variable costs [S1][S9]. But the company has no public record, and its metrics rest solely on company-provided material and are unverified [S11].
2. The price is rich for that risk: $18M at a $72M pre-money implies ~22.5x pre-money ARR and ~47x post-money FY25 revenue versus $15–24M farm-robotics rounds [S4][S11].
3. The exclusivity claim is unproven against real open-field competition (Harvest CROO, plus Advanced Farm Technologies and Traptic unverified) [S2][S3][S6][S11]. Wait; revisit only on verified pick rate, throughput, cash conversion and genuine paid deployments.

## Sources

[S2] Agrobonews: Harvest CROO AI-powered strawberry harvester (B8) — https://www.agrobonews.com/ag-robotics-news/harvest-croo-strawberry-harvester-2026.php
[S3] Harvest CROO Robotics — Technology — https://www.harvestcroorobotics.com/technology
[S4] AgFunderNews: The 7 biggest farm robotics deals of 2024 so far — https://agfundernews.com/the-7-biggest-farm-robotics-deals-of-2024-so-far
[S5] AgFunderNews: Farm robotics' top fundraises in 2025 — https://agfundernews.com/from-experimentation-to-impact-farm-robotics-top-fundraises-in-2025
[S6] The Packer: Harvest CROO touts commercially viable automated strawberry harvesting — https://www.thepacker.com/news/produce-crops/harvest-croo-demonstrates-commercially-viable-automated-strawberry-harvesting
[S7] Octinion: Strawberry Picker (Rubion) — http://octinion.com/strawberry-picker
[S8] The Robot Report: Abundant Robotics shuts down fruit harvesting business — https://www.therobotreport.com/abundant-robotics-shuts-down-fruit-harvesting-business/

Before investing, can Meridian independently verify — via field tests and customer contracts, not the deck — the 94% open-field pick rate at fleet scale, the 1.5 acres/day throughput, that the $3.2M ARR converts to collected cash, and that the two paid deployments are genuine arm's-length contracts rather than discounted pilots?

## Three takeaways

1. The harvest-labor problem is real and independently verified — labor is 50–60% of variable production cost [S1][S9] — so a genuine market exists.
2. The company is a black box: zero public footprint means all traction and economics are unverified deck claims [S11].
3. At a $72M pre-money with active open-field competitors [S2][S3][S6] and a rich price versus comps [S4], the burden of proof sits on Orrin — Wait until primary diligence clears it.
